sustainability-s1.title: New fish added each year at each population size

table.caption: Five indicators measured in one region in 2000 and 2020 (invented data for practice)

options: Meeting present needs while protecting future generations' needs
Using each resource as fast as possible while it lasts
Stopping the use of natural resources to protect them
Growing the economy as fast as possible each year

why.correct: Sustainability balances use today with what is left for the future.
options: Right: present needs, protected future.
Using resources as fast as possible runs them down.
Sustainable use still uses resources, at a rate they can renew.
Economic growth alone says nothing about resources.

items.q: A forest grows about 2,000 cubic meters of new wood a year. Which harvest is sustainable?
options: Cutting about 1,500 cubic meters a year
Cutting about 2,500 cubic meters a year
Cutting about 5,000 cubic meters each year
Cutting the whole forest in one year, then waiting

why.correct: Taking less than the yearly growth leaves the forest at least as large each year.
options: Right: less than the 2,000 m³ the forest adds.
2,500 is more than the forest replaces, so it shrinks.
5,000 a year runs the forest down quickly.
Cutting the whole forest is not a steady harvest.

items.q: A fish population follows logistic growth with a carrying capacity of 6,000 fish. At about what population size can the largest sustainable harvest be taken?
options: About 3,000 fish
About 6,000 fish
About 600 fish
About 12,000 fish

why.correct: For logistic growth, maximum sustainable yield is at about half of carrying capacity: $\frac{6{,}000}{2} = 3{,}000$.
options: Right: half of K.
At K, growth is near zero.
At 600 fish, too few parents produce few young.
The population cannot stay above K.

items.q: Why do many fishery managers set the catch below the calculated maximum sustainable yield?
options: Stock estimates are uncertain and bad years happen, so a margin helps
Catching below MSY makes the fish grow larger than their carrying capacity
Fish caught below MSY sell for a much higher price than fish caught at MSY
MSY is the smallest catch that keeps the fishing fleet in business

why.correct: If the stock is smaller than thought, or a bad year cuts reproduction, a catch at the estimated MSY can push the population down.
options: Right: a safety margin for uncertainty.
No catch level lets a population stay above K.
Price is not why the limit is set below MSY.
MSY is the largest sustainable catch, not the smallest.

items.q: A population is held at 900 fish by a steady harvest; its carrying capacity is 1,000. Compared with holding it at 500, what happens to the sustainable harvest?
options: It is smaller, because a population near K adds few new fish each year
It is larger, because more fish in the lake means more fish to catch each year
It is the same, because the lake has the same carrying capacity either way
It is zero, because a population above half of K is unable to be harvested

why.correct: The sustainable harvest equals the yearly growth, which is much lower near K than at K/2.
options: Right: growth near K is small.
More fish standing does not mean more new fish each year.
Growth depends on population size, not just K.
There is still some growth below K, so some harvest is possible.

items.q: A deer herd has a carrying capacity of 2,400. At what herd size is the maximum sustainable yield taken (assume logistic growth)?

mistakes.why: 2,400 is the carrying capacity, where growth is near zero. MSY is at half of it.
This is not a 10% rule. MSY for logistic growth is at half the carrying capacity.

items.q: Explain why harvesting more than the maximum sustainable yield every year leads to a falling population.

why.correct: Each link: the harvest is larger than the yearly growth, so the population shrinks; a smaller population (below K/2) adds even fewer young; so the same harvest takes a bigger share each year and the decline speeds up.

specific.frame: Because the harvest is ___, the population ___; a smaller population ___, so ___.

cause.label: The harvest
options: larger than the number of fish added each year
smaller than the number of fish added each year
equal to the carrying capacity

why.1: A harvest smaller than growth lets the population grow or hold.
why.2: The carrying capacity is a population size, not a harvest.

effect.label: First effect
options: shrinks
grows
stays the same

why.1: Taking more than is added makes it shrink.
why.2: It stays the same only if harvest equals growth.

mechanism.label: Why it speeds up
options: adds even fewer young each year
adds more young each year
reaches its carrying capacity

why.1: Below K/2, fewer parents mean fewer young.
why.2: A shrinking population moves away from K.

dv.label: Result
options: the decline speeds up until the stock collapses
the population recovers by itself
the harvest can be raised

why.1: It cannot recover while the harvest stays too high.
why.2: Raising the harvest makes the decline worse.

specific.model: Because the harvest is larger than the number of fish added each year, the population shrinks; a smaller population adds even fewer young each year, which leads to the decline speeding up until the stock collapses.

items.q: According to the graph, how many new fish are added each year when the population is 500?
options: 100 fish
500 fish
1,000 fish
50 fish

why.correct: The curve peaks at 100 new fish a year at a population of 500.
options: Right: 100 at the peak.
500 is the population size, not the yearly growth.
1,000 is the carrying capacity.
The curve reaches 100 at 500 fish.

items.q: Why does the curve fall to zero at 1,000 fish?
options: At carrying capacity, crowding and limited food stop growth
At 1,000 fish, the anglers catch each new fish that is born
At 1,000 fish, the fish stop reproducing because they are too old
At 1,000 fish, the lake freezes over and no young survive

why.correct: At K, density-dependent factors (food, space) balance births and deaths, so no new fish are added.
options: Right: limited resources stop growth at K.
The curve shows growth, not catch.
Age is not what sets K.
Freezing is not shown; K reflects limited resources.

items.q: An agency allows a yearly catch of 80 fish from this lake. Write the setup for that catch as a percent of the maximum sustainable yield, then give the answer.

why.correct: $\frac{80}{100} \times 100 = 80\%$ of the maximum sustainable yield, leaving a safety margin.

mistakes.why: Put the catch on top: catch ÷ MSY × 100.
1,000 is the carrying capacity. Compare with the MSY, 100 fish a year.
0.8 is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for the percent.
That compares the catch with K. Compare it with the MSY of 100 fish.

items.q: The lake's population falls to 200 fish after years of overfishing. Using the graph, why is a ban better than a smaller catch while it recovers?
options: At 200 fish the lake adds about 64 fish a year, so any catch slows recovery
At 200 fish the lake adds about 100 fish a year, the most it ever can
At 200 fish the population is above its carrying capacity and will shrink
At 200 fish the population will grow fastest if a few fish are removed

why.correct: Reading the curve at 200 fish gives about 64 new fish a year; letting all of them survive rebuilds the stock fastest.
options: Right: growth is small, so every fish left helps.
The peak of 100 is at 500 fish, not 200.
200 is far below K = 1,000.
Removing fish from a small population slows growth.

items.q: Which indicators in the table changed in a direction that suggests the region is becoming less sustainable?
options: Bird species, forest and groundwater
Grain harvested and the population
Bird species and grain harvested
Forest cover and grain harvested

why.correct: Fewer bird species, less forest and a deeper water table (groundwater being used up) all point away from sustainability.
options: Right: biodiversity, forest and groundwater all worsened.
Grain rose, and population is a driver; the clearest warnings are birds, forest and water.
Grain harvested rose, which on its own is not a warning.
Grain rose; bird species and groundwater are the missing warnings.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in grain harvested per person from 2000 to 2020, then give the answer. (Grain per person = grain ÷ population.)

why.correct: Per person: 2000, $\frac{4.0}{6.0} \approx 0.667$; 2020, $\frac{4.6}{7.5} \approx 0.613$ metric tons. Percent change: $\frac{4.6/7.5 - 4.0/6.0}{4.0/6.0} \times 100 = -8\%$.

mistakes.why: That is the change in total grain (15%). Divide each year's grain by its population first.
Divide by the 2000 value (4.0 / 6.0), the starting point.
15% is the rise in total grain. Per person, grain fell, because population grew faster.
25% is the rise in population. Compute grain per person in each year.

items.q: Total grain rose, but grain per person fell. What does this suggest for the region?
options: Population grew faster than food production, so each person has less food
Food production grew faster than population, so each person has more food
Population fell while food production rose, so food is plentiful
Food production and population grew at the same rate, so nothing changed

why.correct: Grain rose 15% while population rose 25%, so grain per person fell about 8%.
options: Right: population outpaced food.
Population grew faster (25% against 15%).
Population rose from 6.0 to 7.5 million.
They grew at 15% and 25%, not the same rate.

items.q: A fish population with logistic growth starts at 50 fish in a lake with a carrying capacity of 1,000. Put the stages of its yearly growth in order as it grows.
options: Slow growth: few fish to breed
Faster growth: more breeders and plenty of food
Fastest growth: about 500 fish (half of K)
Slowing growth: crowding and less food
Almost no growth: near 1,000 fish

why.correct: Yearly growth rises from a small start, peaks at K/2, then falls to zero at K.
